_why: Capability OBSERVATIONS about the three harnesses, each pinned to the version it was measured on. Codex and Antigravity ship almost daily, so a sentence like 'this flag does not exist' is evidence about one build, never a ruling. npm run harness:usage compares measuredOn with the installed version and prints every observation that is now UNVERIFIED, with the probe that re-settles it. A CONSTRAINT is different: it comes from our own rules or a contract we own, does not lapse with a release, and is listed here only so a reader can tell the two apart. Append; never delete - a lapsed observation gets re-measured and its measuredOn moves.

observations.claim: RE-PROBED on Antigravity 1.2.14 (2026-09-30), and the 1.2.1 split no longer holds for listing. With no command grant, both calls of the re-probe returned an EMPTY response: LISTING (ask for the files in a directory) came back empty, where 1.2.1 returned an accurate listing, and SEARCH (find every file containing a string) came back empty, as before. A session call the same night, with the prompt forbidding the shell, was answered that no non-shell directory listing tool is available. A first run of the same probe read the listing as inconclusive (an answer that was not the accurate listing); the second run returned empty. So on 1.2.14 headless agy with no command grant returned nothing useful for either action in this probe. Not measured: whether a command grant restores the listing, and why the call is empty (the probe records the response, not agy's own stated reason). ROUTING CONSEQUENCE: do not send Antigravity a listing or a search with no grant and expect an answer; enumerate the files yourself and hand it the paths to read, and treat an empty response as a failed delegation. History: on 1.2.1 (2026-09-11) listing worked and was checked against the filesystem (four files, sizes 6, 14, 120 and 17 bytes) while search returned an empty response after 18.2 s with agy printing that a tool needed the command permission headless mode cannot prompt for; on 1.1.28 the same split held; refuted on 1.1.27 without an accuracy check; true on 1.1.25 (2026-09-03), where headless agy auto-denied any tool with no grant, still reported SUCCESS with an empty response, and only read_file, command and write_file were real grant actions (list_dir, grep_search and codebase_search were accepted into settings.json and dropped as invalid).
observations.reprobe: TWO calls, and one alone answers nothing. (1) With no command grant, ask it to LIST a directory: an accurate listing means listing is allowed. (2) With no command grant, ask it to FIND every file containing a string: an empty response means search is still auto-denied. Record the two separately; the actions do not move together.
observations.source: npm run harness:reprobe, ledger lines for this id on 2026-09-30 (probedOn 1.2.14, verdict failed); earlier history: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md, "Three facts about this machine that were not true when this file last said them", and the 2026-09-09 and 2026-09-11 capability re-probes

observations.claim: RE-MEASURED on 0.155.0-alpha.3.7 (2026-09-11): still true, with one sharpening. A run REFUSED for the usage limit still writes a rate_limits snapshot, but its primary and secondary windows are null (limit_id premium, credits balance 0, rate_limit_reached_type null), so harness:usage prints "5-hour window not reported" and "weekly window not reported". The capacity reading is UNKNOWN at exactly the moment the pool is empty, and nothing in the snapshot says the limit was hit. Only the run's own stderr does (`You've hit your usage limit ... try again at <time>`). Codex writes a rate_limits snapshot into its rollout only when one of its own sessions runs, so the capacity reading can be absent or stale; availability is three-valued (headroom / low / UNKNOWN) and is never probed with a paid call.

observations.claim: PARTLY REFUTED, then CORRECTED the same day on 2.1.263. The routing is neither 'always the launcher' nor 'always the session': a subagent's completion notification goes to WHOEVER IS INSIDE A TURN when it fires. Measured both ways. (a) Two probes had a launched session spawn a subagent and stay inside a turn - one explicitly sat in a 120-second blocking command - and the notification arrived in that session, carrying the subagent's final message verbatim. (b) A controlled probe had a launched session spawn one background subagent and END ITS TURN immediately; that notification arrived in the LAUNCHER, and the marker file confirmed the subagent had run, so 'no notification' is not confounded with 'never ran'. (c) In the field, sixteen fan-out reports have strayed to a launcher: seven from one row on 2026-09-08 and eight from another on 2026-09-09. A FAN-OUT IS ALWAYS CASE (b), because a session that has spawned agents has nothing left to do but end its turn and wait - which is why waiting on one never works and why the original observation held in practice for the case that matters. The earlier note here, that this was simply 'REFUTED', was measured correctly and generalised wrongly from the stay-in-turn case alone. Consequence for a launcher: stray reports belong to the row that spawned them - relay them with scripts/relay.mjs rather than acting on them. Previously measured true on 2.1.240 (2026-09-03): a session launched by another session never receives its own subagents' completion notifications; they route to the launcher.
observations.reprobe: Two probes, and they must be run as a PAIR or the answer is half true. From a launched session: (1) spawn a background subagent and stay inside one long blocking call - the notification should arrive in that session at the turn boundary; (2) spawn one and end the turn immediately - it should arrive in the launcher. Confirm the subagent actually ran via a marker file in both cases.
observations.source: .agent-workflows/orchestrator/incidents.md, "the fan-out that waited on notifications that could not arrive"; refuted by the 2026-09-09 capability re-probe, commit 1a51192f

observations.claim: RE-MEASURED on 0.155.0-alpha.3.7 (2026-09-11) by the cheapest probe only: the startup banner of `codex exec` still reads `sandbox: workspace-write [workdir, /tmp, $TMPDIR]`, so the writable set is unchanged. The two-write re-derivation was not run, because the usage limit refused the model call. CONFIRMED with one correction on 0.154.0-alpha.11, re-derived from scratch by a controlled pair of delegations four minutes apart from one session. The writable set is THE LAUNCHING SESSION'S WORKING DIRECTORY PLUS THE TEMP DIRECTORIES, not the working directory alone. Probe A wrote a file under the launching session's own worktree and got every fact in it right. Probe B, same launcher and same flags, was handed two targets in one run: a path in a SIBLING WORKTREE was refused, and the refusal on this build is an OS access error, not a sandbox policy message - verbatim, `New-Item : Access to the path 'C:\claude\NoaCG-Studio\.claude\worktrees\new-session-db1287\.codex-probe-b.txt' is denied.` - while a path under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp in the SAME RUN succeeded. Both outcomes were checked on disk. The mechanism is printed by Codex itself on every run and needs no probing at all: the startup banner of `codex exec` reads `sandbox: workspace-write [workdir, /tmp, $TMPDIR]`. Consequence for a reader of this entry: the temp directory is writable, so a delegation can stage a file it cannot place, and a session that only reads the summary can record a task as attempted while nothing moved. Everything below still holds. A delegation's writable root is THE LAUNCHING SESSION'S WORKING DIRECTORY, and nothing else outside temp. Measured three times on 2026-09-09, and the third attempt CONFIRMS the rule by succeeding. First, handed the ordinary row recipe ('make a feature branch in its own worktree before the work starts'), the delegate was denied writing C:/claude/NoaCG-Studio/.git/refs/heads/<branch> and stopped having changed no file. Then, given a worktree created for it in advance and told to run no git at all, it refused again and said why in plain terms: the target 'is outside that writable root, and approval is disabled', naming the launching session's own worktree as the only writable path. It read both target files correctly and reported its analysis, so reads are unrestricted; only writes are pinned. CONSEQUENCE FOR ROUTING: pre-creating a worktree does NOT help, because the root follows the launcher, not the prompt. A delegation can only edit files under the directory the launching session is sitting in. Either launch it from a session whose cwd IS the worktree the work belongs in, or have it edit in the launcher's own checkout and move the result. Third attempt, launched from a session whose OWN working directory was the target worktree: it created a new module and edited three existing files there without complaint. So the rule is positive as well as negative - delegate from the session that sits where the result belongs and it simply works. This is the mechanical reason such delegations get recorded as attempted and never landed, and it is not fixed by choosing the harness more often.
observations.reprobe: Cheapest first: run any `codex exec` and read the `sandbox:` line of its startup banner, which names the writable set outright. To re-derive it, delegate ONE run that attempts two writes - one into a different worktree, one into the temp directory - and asks for each outcome separately; check both on disk rather than believing the report.
observations.source: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md - the delegate that cannot make its own branch; re-derived and corrected by the 2026-09-09 harness verdict, docs/metrics/2026-09-09-harness-verdict.md

observations.claim: Every `codex exec` starts a fleet of node processes that does NOT exit when the run does, and the cost is memory rather than time. Measured on this laptop: 10 node processes and 619 MB before any delegation, 40 processes and 2554 MB after four wrapper delegations and five plain `codex exec` runs, with codex.exe going from one process to three. Not every invocation leaves a whole family behind, so do not divide those totals: the firm per-delegation figure is the REAP, which freed 778 MB by killing the sixteen processes belonging to four completed delegations - four processes and about 195 MB each. The survivors group by creation time into families of five to seven processes measuring 330-430 MB AT CREATION - a cua_node launch.mjs, an ./mcp/server.mjs, a staging runtime, and an npx `@playwright/mcp` pair worth about 175 MB of it - and each family stays resident long after its own job completes; the oldest on screen was 40 minutes past its work. Budget 195 MB per delegation as the residue and treat 330-430 MB as the peak. The parents are ALIVE, not orphaned: one codex.exe (pid 4264) was holding four separate fleets, one per session it had served. TWO CONSEQUENCES FOR ROUTING. First, this is NOT the delegation wrapper's doing - two of the leaked families came from plain `codex exec` with no wrapper involved, because the three MCP servers are declared globally in ~/.codex/config.toml, so the orchestrator's only contribution is calling Codex more often than a person does. Second, STARTUP is not the problem and should stop being blamed: the whole MCP fleet is worth 1.1-1.4 s (6.78 s with `-c mcp_servers="{}"` against 7.90-8.19 s with it) and exactly zero tokens (12,443 either way), and the wrapper's channel adds about 3 s to an 8 s job.
observations.reprobe: Count node processes and their total working set before and after a `codex exec`, then group the survivors by creation time and check each family's parent with Get-CimInstance Win32_Process. A family still resident after its job's completedAt confirms it.
observations.source: docs/metrics/2026-09-09-harness-verdict.md, question 4; independently corroborated the same night by claude/ab-reap-codex-delegation-tree, which measured 30 processes and 1.4 GB from three delegations that had ended hours earlier

observations.claim: First seen on 0.161.0-alpha.3 (2026-10-02, row BR, jobs task-muqmbqqu-6s5bbp and task-muqmeoeh-j7emqr) and reproduced on 0.162.0-alpha.4 the same day, read-only and write alike: with `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`, every shell command in a CLI session is refused before it runs with `Failed to create unified exec process: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors`. The cause is written in ~/.codex/.sandbox/sandbox.<date>.log: the setup helper validates read/execute access on the desktop runtime's node_repl.exe (AppData/Local/OpenAI/Codex/runtimes/cua_node/<hash>/bin), opens it for an ACL update, and gets os error 32 (file in use); one failed validation fails the whole refresh. The holder is the session itself: the machine config's `node_repl` MCP server and the `unified-computer-use` plugin's `cua_repl` server each start node_repl.exe at session start. Measured with `codex exec -s read-only`: disabling only the node_repl server still fails, `--disable plugins` alone still fails, both together run the command. `-c plugins."unified-computer-use@openai-bundled".enabled=false` does NOT stop cua_repl; `-c mcp_servers={}` does NOT clear the server table (it merges); `-c mcp_servers.<undeclared>.enabled=false` fails the whole config with `invalid transport`. The desktop app's own 0.158.0-alpha.2.1 setup helper does not run the validation, so the same config works there. scripts/codex-rescue.mjs (defect 5) therefore starts every delegation with `--disable plugins` and each listed config MCP server disabled; with that, a read-only probe (list a directory, count package.json lines: 59 entries, 236 lines, both checked) and a write probe (create a file in the worktree, checked on disk) both completed through /rescue on 0.162.0-alpha.4.
observations.reprobe: From a worktree, `codex exec -s read-only` with no overrides on a one-command task: `setup refresh had errors` in the reply and `runtime read/execute validation failed ... node_repl.exe ... os error 32` in ~/.codex/.sandbox/sandbox.<date>.log confirm it still holds; a command that runs refutes it, after which the wrapper's overrides are no longer needed for this reason (they still cut the MCP fleet).
observations.source: docs/HARNESS_ROUTING.md, "Codex: every command refused with setup refresh had errors"; row BZ (claude/bz-codex-rescue-setup)

observations.claim: The Agent tool takes `isolation` (worktree or remote) but no working-directory parameter, so a new subagent starts either in a FRESH worktree or in the launcher's own checkout - never in an existing worktree. And no SendMessage is callable from a main session: the Agent tool's own description tells you to use SendMessage to continue an agent, but the tool is not in the session's tool list. Together they mean an orchestrator can neither ADOPT a dead row's worktree nor WAKE the row that owns it. Measured on row CA of the 2026-09-10 night wave: it stalled holding the only copy of a rebuilt slide deck as uncommitted files in its worktree, and the rescue had to be a new row that copied the files out by path into its own branch.
observations.reprobe: Read the Agent tool's parameter schema for a cwd or working-directory field, and the session's tool list for SendMessage. Either one present refutes the matching half; record the halves separately.
observations.source: the 2026-09-11 deck rescue and the commit that rebuilt the deck

observations.claim: RE-PROBED on Antigravity 1.2.14 (2026-09-30): the plan-instead-of-answer behaviour was not reproduced, and the answer-directly prefix no longer rescues the call. The bare listing prompt (List every file under <dir>, recursively, with each file's size in bytes) through npm run agy:read returned an EMPTY response three times out of three, and none was a plan. The same prompt with the answer-directly prefix did not return the listing either: it returned a sentence saying an exploration subagent had been dispatched to list the files and that the complete list would follow. So on 1.2.14 a read-only listing delegation fails in a different shape, an empty response or a promise of a later answer, and both look like success to a caller that only checks the call status. This is consistent with the listing result recorded under agy-headless-auto-denies-ungranted-tools on the same build. Not measured: why the response is empty, and whether a plain one-file read question still answers directly on 1.2.14. History: on 1.2.1 (2026-09-11) the bare prompt came back as a plan.md three times out of three (12.8 to 13.5 s, about 34 K input tokens each) while the prefixed prompt returned the correct listing once out of once.
observations.reprobe: Run the bare listing prompt above through npm run agy:read three times and count how many return a plan instead of the listing; then the same with the answer-directly prefix.

observations.claim: REFUTED as of 2.1.284 (2026-09-29): wave rows in a cloud session now DO get the GitHub MCP tools of the cloud path of queue-merge.md. Probe, in the first fresh cloud session whose base carried the allowlist change (#524, commit 69e805e; session branch at e910f75): a wave-row-mechanical subagent's ToolSearch select:mcp__github__pull_request_read,mcp__github__create_pull_request,mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge loaded all three, and pull_request_read (method get, NoaCG/NoaCG-Studio #508) returned merged: true, title 'Say at cloud session start when GitHub access is not working'. Only wave-row-mechanical was launched; wave-row and wave-row-deciding carry a byte-identical tools: line but run a different model and were not probed. Three of the eight allowlisted tools were loaded and only a read was exercised: create_pull_request and enable_pr_auto_merge loaded but were not called, and actions_run_trigger, actions_get, actions_list, get_job_logs and disable_pr_auto_merge were not loaded, so a row's first real cloud queue is the first write test. CAUSE, for the record: subagents inherit the host-injected GitHub MCP (no .mcp.json, no user or managed MCP config, no deny rule; a headless claude -p sees 'No MCP servers configured'), and an explicit tools: allowlist filters out every tool it does not name - the old wave-row allowlist named no mcp__github__ tool. Measured on 2.1.284 before the fix: a general-purpose subagent read PR #508 while a wave-row-mechanical subagent got 'No matching deferred tools found'. The 2026-09-28 reading on 2.1.283 (no MCP tools for any subagent) most likely came from the same filter (inferred). The allowlist adds exactly mcp__github__create_pull_request, pull_request_read, actions_run_trigger, actions_get, actions_list, get_job_logs, enable_pr_auto_merge and disable_pr_auto_merge - no wildcard, no merge, push, file-write or branch tool (actions_run_trigger also carries cancel-run and delete-run-logs methods).
observations.reprobe: In a fresh cloud session: launch wave-row-mechanical, ToolSearch select:mcp__github__pull_request_read,mcp__github__create_pull_request,mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge, and read one PR with pull_request_read (no writes); confirm the three wave-row*.md tools: lines are still identical. All three loaded and the read succeeds: this holds. 'No matching deferred tools found': first check that the session branch carries the current definitions (claude-cloud-worktree-base-is-the-session-branch); if it does, try mcp__github__* in a throwaway local copy of the definition, as a diagnostic only and never landed (it would also grant merge, push, file-write and branch tools), before concluding the host stopped injecting the MCP.

observations.claim: In a cloud session, isolation: worktree creates each row's worktree from the primary checkout's HEAD, which is the session's own claude/* branch at the main it was started from, not origin/main; the agent registry (.claude/agents/) is read from that same checkout.
